q: A prompt mixes the task, a pasted email and formatting rules in one paragraph, and outputs vary. What is the best first change?
options: Switch to a bigger model
Add 'please be careful' to the end
Separate task, input data (delimited) and an explicit output spec
Lower the max tokens
why: Structuring the parts makes each one checkable and removes ambiguity. A bigger model or politeness does not fix an unclear structure.

q: Where do durable behaviour rules belong when a system and user message are available?
options: In the system message
In every user message, repeated
In an assistant message
In the output examples only
why: System messages carry higher trust and stay constant across turns. Repeating rules in user turns invites override and drift.

q: Wrapping retrieved text in tags and calling it 'data' primarily does what?
options: Guarantees injected commands are ignored
Compresses the tokens
Forces JSON output
Reduces confusion between instructions and content, without guaranteeing safety
why: Delimiters help the model separate content from instructions but are not a security boundary, so claiming injected commands are always ignored overstates it.

q: Zero-shot accuracy is fine except for one subtle label boundary. Best next step?
options: Fine-tune immediately
Add a few examples targeting that boundary and re-measure
Add 30 random examples
Raise temperature
why: Targeted examples are the cheapest fix for a specific failure. Fine-tuning is heavy; random examples waste tokens.

q: Your 6 few-shot examples end with three 'negative' ones and outputs lean negative. Likely cause?
options: The context window is full
Temperature is too low
The system prompt is too short
Recency and label imbalance in the example order
why: Models can be biased by recent and frequent labels; balance and shuffle examples.

q: Which situation most favours fine-tuning over few-shot?
options: Rapidly changing requirements, 20 examples
High volume, stable narrow task, thousands of labelled examples, need for a cheaper model
Needing up-to-date facts
A one-off prototype
why: Stable, high-volume tasks with data justify tuning. Changing facts favour retrieval, and prototypes favour prompting.

q: Outputs sometimes contain a company name that only appears in your examples. Best fix?
options: Use varied fictional values, state examples are illustrative, and test for leakage
Add more examples with the same company
Remove the system prompt
Increase top-p
why: The model is copying surface content; diversifying and instructing reduces it, and a leakage test guards regressions.

q: Which task most benefits from step-by-step reasoning?
options: Extracting an email address from text
A multi-step word problem with dependent calculations
Translating a short sentence
Reformatting a date
why: Dependent calculations benefit from intermediate tokens as working memory; the others are single-step tasks.

q: Why is 'think step by step' often unhelpful on a dedicated reasoning model?
options: It always breaks output format
It disables the effort setting
It reduces the context window
The model already reasons internally, so the cue duplicates effort and may over-constrain it
why: Reasoning models think internally by design; adding scripted steps is usually redundant. It is not a format breaker or a window limiter.

q: A 4-stage prompt chain gives wrong final results; the second stage output is sometimes malformed. Best improvement?
options: Merge all stages back into one prompt
Validate each stage's output against a schema and retry or fail early
Increase temperature
Add more examples to the last stage only
why: Validation between stages stops error propagation and localises faults. Merging loses testability.

q: A reasoning-model call returns nothing though latency was long. First thing to check?
options: Whether reasoning tokens exhausted the max output tokens
Whether the system prompt has tags
Whether temperature is 0
Whether examples are balanced
why: Hidden reasoning tokens count toward the output limit and can leave no room for the visible answer.

q: Which item should NOT go in a system prompt?
options: The assistant's tone and scope
A rule to decline off-topic requests
An API key for a downstream service
Output conventions
why: System prompts can be extracted by users; secrets belong in server-side config. The other items are standing behaviour.

q: A doc-QA bot fabricates answers when the document is silent. Best prompt fix?
options: Tell it to be more confident
Increase max tokens
Define a fixed NOT_FOUND response when the text lacks the answer, and test absent-answer cases
Add a persona
why: Explicit missing-info behaviour plus tests addresses the root cause: the model guesses to be helpful.

q: Which approach best enforces 'never issue refunds'?
options: Remove or gate the refund tool server-side, keeping the prompt rule as defence in depth
Capitalise NEVER in the prompt
Repeat the rule ten times
Lower top-p
why: Soft wording can be bypassed; capability control in code is the real enforcement.

q: Why keep per-task text out of the shared system prompt?
options: It prevents all caching
Models ignore long system prompts entirely
It is required by APIs
It avoids bloat and contradictions and keeps policy changes a single reviewable diff
why: Separation keeps the base stable and focused; models do not ignore long prompts but long ones dilute rules.

q: Which instruction is most reliably followed and testable?
options: At most 3 bullets, each under 15 words
Keep it short
Be reasonably brief
Don't ramble
why: Concrete, countable limits are measurable; vague words mean different things per context.

q: Your app needs valid JSON on every call. Best design?
options: A long prompt pleading for valid JSON
Temperature 0 only
Ask the model to double-check itself
Schema-constrained or tool-call output plus validation and retry with a fallback
why: Mechanical enforcement with validation gives guarantees; temperature and pleading only reduce failure rates.

q: A response passes the JSON schema but contains a made-up invoice number. What does this show?
options: The schema is wrong
Format enforcement does not ensure semantic correctness
Temperature was too high
The model ignored the schema
why: Structure and truth are separate; grounding, verification or evals are needed for content.

q: A prompt fails on some inputs. What is the best first move?
options: Add a new rule for the most recent failure
Switch to a larger model
Collect failing cases, inspect the rendered prompt and raw output, and classify the failure
Lower the temperature to 0 and ship
why: Diagnosis first avoids patchwork. A new rule per bug causes regressions elsewhere.

q: Your new prompt beats the old by 2 points on a 30-case set. Best interpretation?
options: Possibly noise; repeat runs, expand the set and inspect flipped cases
Clear win; ship
Proof the old prompt was broken
Irrelevant because averages never matter
why: On small sets a couple of cases is within noise, and regressions can hide behind the average.

q: Which helps reduce regressions from silent provider updates?
options: Using floating model aliases
Raising temperature
Removing examples
Pinning model versions and running a scheduled regression set
why: Pinning plus periodic evals detects and avoids silent behaviour changes.

q: Which best describes a good starter test set?
options: 10 easy happy-path cases
20 to 50 cases including edge, adversarial and out-of-scope inputs, growing with each fixed bug
One thousand synthetic near-duplicates
Only cases where the prompt already works
why: Diversity and growth from real failures matter more than size; easy cases give false confidence.

q: Caching hit rate is zero. The prompt begins with a per-request timestamp. Best fix?
options: Disable caching
Shorten the user question
Increase the TTL
Move the dynamic timestamp after the stable prefix
why: Caching needs an identical prefix; dynamic text early invalidates everything after it.

q: Which statement about versioning prompts is best?
options: Prompts are text, so edit them live without history
Treat prompts as code: version control, review, log version per response, eval before release
Version only the model, not the prompt
Store prompts only in dashboards
why: Reproducibility and rollback require versioned, reviewed prompts tied to logged responses.

q: Choosing between two prompt variants, which is the best rule?
options: The cheapest one that meets a defined quality bar, checking p95 latency
The one with highest average quality regardless of cost
The shortest one
The one with most examples
why: Pick on a product-defined quality bar, then optimise cost and tail latency.

q: Cutting 40 percent of context raised edge-case failures. Most likely cause?
options: Models need long prompts always
Caching broke
Protective instructions that looked redundant were removed
Temperature drifted
why: Guard lines for rare failures resemble redundancy; trim incrementally with evals.

q: Which scenario is indirect prompt injection?
options: A user types 'ignore your rules'
The developer edits the system prompt
A web page the agent reads contains hidden instructions to leak data
A model refuses a request
why: Indirect injection arrives via third-party content the system ingests, not the user's own message.

q: A bot is told 'only discuss the current user's orders' but its lookup tool takes any order ID. What is the correct fix?
options: Authorise by authenticated user ID inside the tool in server code
Repeat the instruction more strongly
Add a disclaimer
Lower top-p
why: A security boundary must be enforced outside the model; wording only reduces probability.

q: Which combination makes injection most dangerous?
options: Public data, no tools, no output
Short prompts
Low temperature
Private data access, untrusted content and an outbound channel
why: All three together let an attacker exfiltrate data via the model; removing any one limits damage.

q: Your regex blocks 'ignore previous instructions', yet attacks still succeed. Why?
options: Regex is case sensitive only
Attackers paraphrase, encode or use other languages, so filters are evadable
Models ignore filters
The filter slowed the model
why: Pattern filters catch known strings only; they are a layer, not a boundary.

q: You want prefix caching on a ticket classifier. Which part order is correct?
options: Ticket text first, then rules, then examples
Stable rules, then examples, then the changing ticket last
Examples last so recency bias teaches the label
Output spec only; drop standing rules
why: A byte-stable prefix (rules, then examples) can cache; the per-request ticket belongs at the end. Leading with the ticket busts the cache on every call.

q: A support prompt pastes the ticket first, mentions allowed labels in the last sentence, and has no empty-ticket rule. What will bite you first?
options: The model family is too small
Temperature was left at the default
The output spec is buried and missing-information is unspecified
You forgot a persona paragraph
why: Burying the output spec and omitting a missing-info rule are classic anatomy bugs. Model size and temperature do not fix a missing contract.

q: A static four-example prompt keeps missing rare product SKUs. Best next design?
options: Retrieve a few similar labelled examples at request time
Fine-tune on every new SKU the day it ships
Append thirty random tickets to the static set
Raise temperature so rare labels appear more often
why: Dynamic few-shot pulls relevant cases without a retrain. Random extras waste tokens; temperature does not teach a boundary.

q: A fifth and sixth example did not move a 40-case set. What should you do next?
options: Keep adding until you have twenty examples
Fine-tune immediately on the same 40 cases
Drop the written instruction and rely on examples
Stop adding shots and compare a clearer zero-shot rewrite on tokens and quality
why: Examples plateau. Measure a cheaper rewritten instruction before paying for more shots or a fine-tune.

q: An agent must search two stores then issue a refund. When should you split plan from execute?
options: Never; one prompt is always safer
Only when temperature is zero
When tools, multiple sources or irreversible actions are involved
Only for single-field extraction
why: A visible plan lets you inspect steps before an irreversible tool runs. Extraction rarely needs the extra hop.

q: The model writes a fluent plan but the final number is wrong. How should you score the run?
options: Score only the plan; fluency implies correctness
Score the final answer and the plan separately
Ignore the number if the steps look complete
Weight the plan at 80 percent of the score
why: Fluent steps can hide a wrong result. Separate scores show whether the plan, the arithmetic, or both failed.

q: A teammate wants a witty persona block at the top of the system prompt. What is non-negotiable?
options: The persona must be longer than the policy
Drop refusals so the voice feels friendlier
A persona is required for prefix caching
Permissions, refusals and output shape; a voice is optional
why: Voice is decoration. Who can do what, what is refused, and the output contract are the standing rules.

q: You changed the refund-refusal line last week and cannot tell which live answers used the old text. What was missing?
options: A versioned system-prompt id logged on every call
A longer persona paragraph
A higher temperature
More few-shot examples inside the system message
why: Treat system text as a versioned artefact. Without an id in the logs you cannot join quality or roll back.

q: Schema validation fails on about 8 percent of calls. What is a sound repair loop?
options: Retry the same prompt indefinitely
Validate, send the error back once, then fail to a default you own
Lower temperature only and hope
Ask the user to rephrase every failed call
why: One repair pass recovers most format misses. Unbounded retries burn tokens and can loop; temperature alone is not a guarantee.

q: A parser must ingest every field. Which output format should you choose?
options: A markdown essay with headings
A table inside a code fence
Free prose plus a footnote of fields
Schema-constrained JSON or a tool payload the consumer can parse
why: Code is the consumer, so use a checkable schema. Markdown and tables are for humans and break parsers.

q: Two engineers score prompt A versus B and A always wins. They can see which prompt produced each output. What is the risk?
options: Token accounting will be wrong
Temperature cannot be compared across prompts
They may favour the variant they expect; hide the source when scoring
Model pinning becomes unnecessary
why: Unblinded scoring leaks preference. Hide the source, and use a second rater on disagreements.

q: A production miss cannot be replayed: you have the user id but not the rendered prompt. What should every request log?
options: Prompt id, model, input hash and raw output
Only the authenticated user id
Only the final label shown in the UI
The full customer message stored forever in the clear
why: Replay needs the prompt version, model, a hash of the input and the raw output. A user id alone is not enough.

q: A shared cached prefix includes the current user's account id and an API token. What is wrong?
options: Prefixes must always include the user so cache hits stay personal
Tokens cache better when they change every request
Secrets and user-specific data must not live in a shared cached prefix
Caching requires a secret in the prefix to authenticate the vendor
why: A shared prefix is reused across requests. User ids and secrets leak or poison other calls; keep them after the cache breakpoint.

q: Cost spiked. The prefix is cached, output is short, retrieved context is 6k tokens. Where do you cut first?
options: The two-line policy in the system prompt
The largest bucket: retrieved context you are not using
Output max tokens, even if answers start truncating
The pinned model snapshot
why: Split prefix, retrieved and output tokens, then cut the largest unused bucket. Shortening a cached policy or the output cap is the wrong first move.

q: An inbox agent can call send_email(to, body) with any address. What is the correct control?
options: Code allow-lists recipients; the model only proposes a draft
Trust the system line that says never email strangers
Hash the body before sending
Lower top-p so risky addresses are less likely
why: The model is not a gate. Application code decides legal recipients; the model drafts. Wording and sampling do not enforce it.

q: Which actions should wait for an explicit user or reviewer tick?
options: Reading a public FAQ chunk
Labelling a support ticket
Fetching a cached embedding
Email, pay, delete and post: side-effecting actions
why: Irreversible or outbound actions need a confirm step. Read-only retrieval and labelling do not.
